transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for calling S-Net technical support, my name is Alex. May I please have the account number on the line so I can pull up the record?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hi Alex. Yeah, the account number is 884-291-002. The name on the account is Marcus Delgado, if that helps.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Perfect, thank you Marcus. I've got the account pulled up here on my screen. I'm showing gigabit fiber at the service address, installed about fourteen months ago. What can I help you with today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, so, I'll be honest with you, I'm incredibly frustrated at this point. I've got your gigabit internet plan, and about two weeks ago I bought a new mesh Wi-Fi system because the single router wasn't covering the back half of the house. Ever since then, and especially over the last three days, the connection just randomly drops completely for about thirty seconds, roughly once an hour. And it always seems to happen in the middle of a call. I got kicked out of a client presentation yesterday afternoon and I had to dial back in on my phone hotspot, which was embarrassing.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Marcus, I am so sorry to hear that, and I want you to know that getting kicked out of a client presentation is exactly the kind of thing that should not be happening on a gigabit connection. I can completely understand how disruptive and honestly how stressful that is, especially when you're working from home and your income depends on those calls being stable. I'm going to take ownership of this one personally, and we are going to work through it together until we understand exactly what is causing those disconnects.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I appreciate that, I really do. I've called in twice before about slowness and both times I got bounced around, so I'm hoping today is different. I just need this actually fixed, not a ticket number.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's fair, and I hear you. No ticket numbers and no transfers today if I can help it. Let me start by making sure I've got the full picture correct before I touch anything on the line, because I don't want to change settings based on a wrong assumption.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Sure, go ahead.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: So, to make sure I understand the scope of this properly: you're using the S-Net fiber modem we installed, but you've now added your own third-party mesh Wi-Fi system behind it. The entire network — not one device, but everything in the house — loses internet access for roughly thirty seconds at a time, about once an hour, and this started around the time the mesh system went in. Is that an accurate summary?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, that's exactly right. And it's the whole house, because when it happens my wife's laptop downstairs drops too, and the smart TV buffers. So it's not just my office.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That is a very useful detail, because it tells me this is almost certainly not a single-device or single-room problem. When the drop happens, does anything change visually on the equipment? A light changing color, anything like that?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yeah, actually. The light on the main mesh node turns red when it happens. Then after maybe thirty seconds it goes back to white and everything reconnects on its own without me doing anything.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Red to white, and it self-recovers. Okay. And when that main mesh node turns red, does the light on our S-Net modem change at all, or does it stay solid?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Honestly I've never checked. The modem's in the utility closet off the garage and I'm always at my desk when it happens.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: No problem at all. Would you be able to walk over there now? I'd like to know what the modem is showing while we're on the line, because that single data point tells us whether the problem is upstream from the modem or between the modem and your mesh system.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Sure, give me just a moment. I'm going to put you on speaker and walk over.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Take your time, Marcus, I'm right here.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, I'm in the closet now. The modem has four lights and they're all solid green. Nothing blinking, nothing red, nothing amber.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That is genuinely helpful. Four solid greens means the fiber signal coming in from the street to the modem is locked and stable, and the modem is authenticated with our network. If the problem were on our side of the wall, I'd expect at least one of those lights to be cycling or amber. So the fault is very likely sitting between the modem and your new mesh router.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Huh. But they're plugged directly into each other, there's nothing in between.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Understood, and that's actually a good thing — fewer variables. Can you describe the cable that's running between the modem and the mesh router? Is it the yellow ethernet cable our technician left, or a different one?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's a flat black one. It came in the box with the mesh system. I used that one because I wanted it to look cleaner running along the baseboard.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Totally understandable, and those flat cables usually work fine. But since we're here, let's rule it out. Could you unplug it from both the modem and the router, take a quick look at the gold pins inside each connector to make sure none of them are bent or pushed in, and then plug both ends back in firmly until you hear a click?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yep, doing it now. Unplugging from the router end... pins look fine, all eight of them are lined up. Unplugging from the modem end... that one looks fine too. Okay, plugging both back in. I heard the click on both ends.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Great. Now, because we just interrupted that link, the mesh router is going to need a moment to re-establish. While we wait on that, can you tell me the exact brand and model of the mesh system you bought?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's a Netgear Orbi. The model number on the bottom is RBK752. It came as a three pack, so one main router and two satellites.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Okay, the RBK752. That's a solid system, I have no concerns about the hardware quality itself. Marcus, are you seeing the mesh light come back yet?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's pulsing white right now. Still pulsing. Hang on... okay, now it's solid white.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Perfect. Now I want to explain something that I think may be at the root of this, because I'd rather you understand what's happening than just have me flip switches silently. There's a condition called Double NAT. Our S-Net modem has a router built into it, and your Orbi is also a full router. So you've got two devices in a row, both trying to hand out IP addresses and both trying to manage the same traffic. Most of the time they tolerate each other, but every so often they disagree about who owns a connection, and when they do, the downstream device drops everything and rebuilds the table. That rebuild takes about thirty seconds.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, that actually lines up scarily well with what I'm seeing. Thirty seconds is exactly it.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It does line up. The fix is to put our modem into what's called Bridge Mode, which switches off its routing functions entirely and lets it act as a plain pass-through. Your Orbi then becomes the only router in the house and there's nobody left to argue with. I can push that configuration change from my side right now.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay. Will that knock me offline while it happens?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It will reboot the modem, yes.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Right, but for how long? I've got a call at the top of the hour I really can't miss.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It shouldn't be too bad. Let's just push it and see where we land, and if anything looks off we'll deal with it from there. Are you okay for me to go ahead?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I mean... I guess so. Go ahead.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Sending the command to your modem now. You should see the lights drop in just a few seconds.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yep, lights just went out. It's dark. Okay, now one light is blinking.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's the fiber sync coming back up. Let it do its thing.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: While we're waiting — is this something you all should have caught when the install happened? Because nobody mentioned any of this to me.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's a fair question and I won't dodge it. At the time of install you didn't have a third-party router, so Double NAT wasn't a factor then. It only became one when the Orbi went in. That said, I do think our documentation could make this clearer for customers who add their own mesh systems later, and I'm going to note that on the account.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Fair enough. I appreciate you not blaming the previous guy.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Not my style, and it wouldn't help you anyway. Now, while this reboots, let me ask about placement. You mentioned two satellites. How far is the nearest satellite from the main Orbi router?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The first one is in the hallway right outside my office, maybe forty feet from the main unit, through two interior walls. The second one is out in the garage, that one's further, maybe seventy feet.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Forty feet through two interior walls is generally workable. Seventy feet out to a garage is where I'd start to worry, because garage walls often have metal studs, insulation backing, or ductwork running through them, and any of those will degrade the wireless backhaul between the satellite and the main unit. Here's the question that would help me narrow it down: when the drop happens, do devices connected directly to the main router drop as well, or is it only the devices on the satellites?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: You know, that's a really good question and I'm not sure. I'm always in my office when I notice it, and my office is on the hallway satellite. I assumed the TV downstairs drops too but I'd have to actually check.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's an honest answer and it's more useful than a guess. Let's keep that as an open thread and come back to it. Is the modem back up yet?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Checking... yes, four solid green lights again. And the Orbi just went solid white, so I think we're connected.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Excellent, Marcus, that was quicker than it could have been. Now Bridge Mode is active, which means the Orbi is the only router in the house. Let's verify the line is actually performing. Are you able to open a web browser on your work laptop?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yeah, browser's open.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Please go to speedtest dot net and run the default test for me, then tell me the download and upload numbers.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Running it now... okay. Download is 847 megabits, upload is 41.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That is a healthy result for a gigabit plan over Wi-Fi. For context, yesterday's diagnostic on your line showed your throughput topping out in the low four hundreds, so the Double NAT conflict was very likely choking your bandwidth as well as causing the drops. What were you typically seeing before today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yeah, I was getting like four hundred, four twenty on a good day. I just figured that was normal for Wi-Fi.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It's common, but it isn't normal on fiber. So that's one real improvement locked in. However, I don't want to declare victory yet, because faster throughput doesn't automatically mean we've stopped the intermittent drop, and the drop is the thing that's actually hurting you.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Right, exactly. The speed was never really my complaint. It's the dropping that's killing my meetings.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Agreed. So here's what I'd like to do next. I'm going to run a continuous ping test from our edge server directly to your modem. It sends one small packet every second and measures whether any of them fail to come back. If there's any instability left on the physical path, packet loss will expose it. Are you alright with me running that?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yeah, go for it.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Starting it now. Marcus, I'm going to place you on a brief hold while that test collects a sample and while I check something in our provisioning system. You'll hear music, but I promise I'm still working on this. I'll come right back to you.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No problem.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thanks for holding, Marcus, I appreciate your patience. Two things came back. First, the ping test returned zero percent packet loss, which tells me the physical path from our network to your modem is clean. Second, I checked your provisioning record and the bridge configuration committed successfully on our side, so that's confirmed rather than assumed.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, good. So what's left?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: What's left is everything on your side of the modem, which is the Orbi and its satellites. And that's actually where I'd put my money at this point. Remind me what model that Orbi is again?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: ...The RBK752. I told you that earlier.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Right, of course, the 752. Thank you. On those units there's a known issue on older firmware where the main router loses sync with its satellites and tears down the backhaul link, and the symptom is a disconnect lasting roughly twenty to forty seconds before it heals itself.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That sounds exactly like what I've got.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It does. Can you open the Orbi app on your phone and look at the main screen for me? It usually flags firmware status right at the top.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Opening it... okay, yeah. There's a banner at the top that says firmware out of date. It says version 4.6.14.3 is available.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: There we go. Outdated firmware on mesh systems is notorious for causing precisely the kind of random thirty-second disconnect you described, especially in the communication between the main router and the satellites rather than between the router and the internet. That's why the modem lights looked perfectly fine to you — because as far as our equipment was concerned, nothing was ever wrong.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That makes sense. Should I hit update?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, please go ahead and start the update.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, hitting update now. It says it's downloading. Do I need to stay near it, or can I walk away? And roughly how long is this going to have me down for?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Just let it run and we'll see. It'll come back when it's ready.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Alright. It's saying the routers will restart when it finishes.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Right. While that's going, let me get a couple of housekeeping details so I can document this properly. What's the best callback number to reach you on?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: 555-0142, got it, thank you. And going back to that open thread from earlier — the satellite in the garage. I'd like you to try something once the firmware finishes. Move that garage satellite from wherever it's sitting now to somewhere with a clearer line of sight, ideally not on the floor and not behind metal shelving.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's on a metal shelf right now, actually. Sitting on top of a toolbox.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That is almost the worst possible surface for it. Metal directly under and behind a wireless unit reflects and absorbs the signal in a way that will absolutely degrade the backhaul. If you can get it up onto a wooden shelf or mounted on a wall, away from the metal, you should see that satellite hold a much stronger link.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, I can move it to the workbench, that's wood. I'll do that after we're done.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That'd be great. And one more thing on placement — is the main Orbi router sitting right next to the modem in the utility closet?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yeah, they're side by side on the same shelf in there.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's fine for the wired link, but bear in mind that closet is now the center of your wireless coverage, and it sounds like it's at one end of the house rather than the middle. Long term, if you ever run a wall plate or a longer ethernet run, moving the main router closer to the middle of the floor plan would improve everything. That's not today's fix, just something to keep in your back pocket.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Noted. Actually that closet is the far corner of the house, so that probably explains some of the coverage complaints from my wife.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: It very likely does. How's the firmware update looking?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It says installing on the main router now. Satellite one says pending.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Good, that's the expected sequence — the main unit flashes first, then it pushes to each satellite in turn. Let's let it finish.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: This has been a nightmare for my work, honestly. Two weeks of looking unreliable on calls.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I know, and I don't want to minimize that. It's incredibly stressful when the technology gets in the way of your livelihood and you can't tell anyone why it keeps happening. For what it's worth, the fact that you noticed the thirty-second pattern and that it started around the mesh install is what let us narrow this down as fast as we did.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I appreciate you saying that.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Marcus, I'm going to put you on a short hold one more time while I add detailed notes to your account and flag the line for monitoring on our end. Is that alright?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yeah, that's fine.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you for waiting. I've documented the bridge mode change, the firmware issue, and the satellite placement recommendation on the account, so if you ever do need to call back, the next agent will see exactly what we did today instead of starting from zero. I've also flagged your line so our system will alert us automatically if it sees repeated session drops over the next week.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, that's reassuring. Update just finished, by the way. Both satellites say up to date and the main light is pulsing white.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Perfect. Let it settle until that light goes solid.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Still pulsing... still pulsing... okay, it's solid white now. And satellite one just went solid blue, which I think is good.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Solid blue on an Orbi satellite means a strong backhaul link to the main router, so that's exactly what we want to see. Let's do a final round of verification. First, can you load a couple of different websites on the laptop and tell me how they feel?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Let me check... YouTube loaded instantly. A news site loaded instantly. Everything feels snappy, honestly snappier than it did before.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Good. Now let's test the thing you actually care about, which is call stability. Could you start a video call — even just a test meeting with yourself — and leave it running for a minute or two while we talk?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yeah, starting one now... okay I'm in a meeting room by myself. Video's up, it says my connection is strong.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let's give that a moment while it holds. In the meantime, can I confirm the account number for the notes?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Alex, that's the third thing I've given you twice now. It's 884-291-002.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: You're right, my apologies, I should have had that in front of me. 884-291-002, thank you, and I won't ask again.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It's alright. The meeting's still running, by the way, no drop. Connection indicator is still green.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's a good sign, though I want to be straight with you rather than overselling it: a couple of minutes without a drop doesn't prove it on its own, given your pattern was roughly once an hour. What I can tell you with confidence is that we removed two known causes — the Double NAT conflict and the outdated mesh firmware — and either one of those alone could produce exactly your symptom.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's fair. So what do I do if it happens again?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Here's what I'd like you to do. Move that garage satellite off the metal shelf today. Then over the next few days, if you do get another drop, note the time and check whether the downstairs TV drops at the same moment. If everything drops together, it's the main router or the modem link, and we'll go down a hardware path. If only your office drops, it's the hallway satellite's backhaul, and we'll look at placement or adding a wired connection to it.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, that's actually a clear plan. I can do that.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And because your line is flagged for monitoring now, if our system sees repeated drops we may reach out to you before you even call us.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That'd be a first, honestly, in a good way.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let's hope we don't need it. How's that meeting holding up?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Still connected. Five minutes or so now with no interruption, and normally I'd have seen at least one by now given how often it's been happening.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Good. So, Marcus, just to confirm before I let you go — as things stand right now, your internet is up, your speeds are back where they should be for the plan you're paying for, your mesh system is on current firmware, and the meeting you're in has stayed connected. Are you satisfied that the issue you called about is resolved?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes. As far as I can tell right now, it's resolved. And I know what to look for if it comes back, which is honestly more than I had before.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: That's exactly what I was hoping to hear. I really appreciate you walking out to that closet and doing the hands-on parts with me — that's what made this solvable in one call instead of three.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Well, I appreciate you actually explaining what was going on. The last two times I called, nobody told me anything.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I'm glad today was different. Before I let you go, is there absolutely anything else at all I can help you with on the account today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, I think we're all good. You've been extremely helpful.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you so much, Marcus. We do value your feedback, so please stay on the line for a brief one-question survey about my service today. Thank you for choosing S-Net, and have a wonderful rest of your day.
